title: Biblical and rabbinic
hookLine: laws from the Torah and laws from the rabbis carry different weight

cards: On each night of Hanukkah, before the candles are lit, a blessing is said. It thanks God, who made us holy with commandments and commanded us to light the Hanukkah light. Commanded us.
Here's the puzzle: open the Torah from beginning to end and you won't find Hanukkah in it. The story belongs to a much later time. So where exactly did God command it?
The Talmud asks that very question, out loud, in tractate Shabbat. The answer opens up a distinction Jewish law leans on, day after day.

teach.h: FROM THE TORAH, FROM THE RABBIS.
teach.b: D'oraita. It's an Aramaic word meaning from the Torah, and it names a law that comes from the Torah itself. Its partner is d'rabbanan, from the rabbis: a law the sages set.
First, the difference in source. Keeping the Sabbath, eating matzah on the first night of Passover: the Talmud treats these as d'oraita, from the verses.
Lighting Hanukkah candles, and many of the fences you met yesterday: d'rabbanan. Second, the puzzle.
If Hanukkah is rabbinic, how can the blessing say God commanded us? The Talmud gives two answers, from two sages.
One points to Deuteronomy, where the people are told not to turn aside from what the judges of their day teach them.
The other points to a verse in the Song of Moses: ask your father, and he will tell you; your elders, and they will say.
Either way, the rabbis' rulings carry authority because the Torah itself sends people to their teachers. Rabbinic law isn't a stranger; it's a command to listen.
Third, the weights really are different, and you see it when things are unclear.
The Talmud's working rule: in doubt about a Torah law, lean strict. In doubt about a rabbinic law, you may lean lenient. Fourth, why it matters on an ordinary day.
Knowing the source tells you how to act when life gets messy: when you're unsure, when there's illness, when two duties collide.
A rule's weight depends on where it came from.

how: When a rabbi answers a question of Jewish law, the source of the rule matters: a doubt about a Torah law is usually resolved strictly, and a doubt about a rabbinic law may be resolved leniently. The Hanukkah blessing is said over a rabbinic command.

games.q: you're about to light Hanukkah candles and say 'who commanded us'. a friend says: Hanukkah isn't in the Torah. what's the Talmud's answer?
o: the Torah tells people to follow their sages, so the command reaches through them.
Hanukkah is hidden in the Torah in code.
games.why: in tractate Shabbat, one sage cites 'do not turn aside' from what the judges teach; another, 'ask your father, and he will tell you'.

practice: Pick one rule in your own life, a household rule, a promise you keep, a habit you treat like law, and ask where it comes from. Is it close to the ground of who you are, or a fence added later to protect that ground?
Notice, too, whether you'd lean strict or easy if you were ever unsure about it.

wordCard.voice: D'oraita. Aramaic for from the Torah: a law that comes from the Torah itself, set beside d'rabbanan, a law from the rabbis. Today's word.
